title: Optimal robust single-qubit gates in superconducting quantum processors
authors: Tangyou Huang, Anuj Aggarwal, Jingjun Zhu, Akshay Gaikwad, David Niepce, Marcus Rommel, Andreas Nylander, Amr Osman, Anita Fadavi Rousari, Janka Biznárová, Stéphane Guérin, Gheorghe Sorin Paraoanu, Anton Frisk Kockum, Giovanna Tancredi
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires high-fidelity quantum gates that are resilient to control errors and device imperfections. Here, we develop energy-optimal control pulses for single-qubit gates that are simultaneously robust against frequency detuning and waveform inhomogeneities while also suppressing leakage outside the computational subspace. Combining the optimized pulse envelopes with an adaptive control scheme, we experimentally demonstrate optimal robust gates on a superconducting quantum processor. For a gate duration of 90ns, we achieve fidelities above 99.9% for the X gate and 99.6% for Hadamard-type gates. For the X gate, we maintain fidelities above 99.5% for simultaneous drive-amplitude variations up to 20% and qubit detuning up to 4 MHz. This robustness outperforms that of conventional Gaussian pulses by an order of magnitude, without much difference in peak gate fidelity. These results establish a route towards robust single-qubit control in large-scale quantum processors, advancing the development of fault-tolerant quantum computing.
summary: This paper introduces Time-rescaling robust inverse-optimal (TRIO) pulses for single-qubit gates on superconducting quantum processors. The method designs pulses that are inherently robust against common errors like frequency detuning and amplitude fluctuations. Experimentally, these pulses demonstrate significantly superior fidelity maintenance compared to standard Gaussian pulses, paving a practical path toward fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_problem: Developing high-fidelity, robust single-qubit gates for fault-tolerant quantum computation that are resilient to control errors and device imperfections.
main_result: The proposed Time-rescaling robust inverse-optimal (TRIO) pulses achieve fidelities above 99.9% for the X gate and maintain high fidelity even under significant simultaneous drive-amplitude and detuning variations, outperforming conventional Gaussian pulses.
method: The authors use energy-optimal control theory combined with a time-rescaling technique (TRIO) to design pulses that are robust against systematic errors, which are then experimentally validated using Interleaved Randomized Benchmarking (IRB) and Quantum Process Tomography (QPT).
model_or_system: The work is performed on superconducting quantum processors using transmon qubits. The dynamics are modeled using a driven two-level system Hamiltonian, and the control pulses are designed to implement specific unitary gates (X, Hadamard) while minimizing energy.
key_observables: Gate fidelity (measured via IRB), gate infidelity as a function of amplitude error ($\alpha$) and detuning error ($\delta$), and leakage population $P(|2angle)$.
important_parameters: Gate duration ($t_f = 90 	ext{ ns}$), amplitude variation up to 20%, and qubit detuning up to 4 MHz.
main_assumptions: The initial energy-optimal pulses derived from the RIO framework are assumed to be converted into experimentally feasible, smooth waveforms using the TRIO time-rescaling.
figures_summary: Figures compare the pulse envelopes and state trajectories of TRIO vs. Gaussian pulses, and show IRB measurements demonstrating that TRIO maintains higher fidelity across wider error parameter ranges ($\alpha$ and $\delta$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the need for robust gates, detailing the TRIO pulse design methodology, presenting experimental characterization using IRB and QPT, and finally demonstrating the superior robustness of the new pulse scheme compared to existing methods.
why_interesting: The focus on robust control pulses directly addresses the primary bottleneck in scaling quantum processors: maintaining gate fidelity in the presence of unavoidable hardware noise and control imperfections.

Comparison of TRIO (blue) and Gaussian (purple) pulses for an X gate in a two-level system. a, Pulse envelopes; dark and light blue denote the real (dark blue) and imaginary (light blue) components of the TRIO pulse, respectively. b, Corresponding trajectories in the (θ, γ) plane, where θ and γ denote the mixing angle and global phase of the evolving state, respectively. c, State trajectories on the Bloch sphere. Solid curves represent ideal control, whereas dashed curves include a simultaneous 20 % drive-amplitude offset and a 4 MHz detuning error. Filled circles mark the final states of the dashed trajectories.

Experimental characterization of the X gate. a, Reference and interleaved randomized benchmarking decay curves, yielding gate fidelities of 99.94(1) % for the Gaussian pulse and 99.90(1) % for the TRIO pulse, averaged over ten experiments. b, Absolute values of the real and imaginary components of ∆J for the TRIO-based X gate, i.e., the difference between the experimentally reconstructed and ideal X-gate Choi matrices. c, Gate infidelity as a function of gate duration for the Gaussian and TRIO pulses, compared with the coherence limit [37] (solid curve).

Figure 2 presents the benchmarking of the TRIO-based X gate and its Gaussian counterpart for a gate duration of tf = 90 ns. All reported gate fidelities for both Gaussian and TRIO pulses include calibrated DRAG (derivative removal by adiabatic gate) corrections [9]. IRB measurements averaged over five indepen- dent experiments yield X-gate fidelities of F = 99.90 ± 0.01 % for the TRIO pulse and 99.94 ± 0.01 % for the Gaussian pulse, as shown in Fig. 2(a).
